title: SIRE — Student Insight & Recommendation Engine
tagline: A permission-scoped, citation-backed RAG system that helps academic advisors turn SIS/LMS records into reviewable student insights.
summary: SIRE retrieves a student's academic evidence, builds a cited strengths/weaknesses/engagement profile, and proposes recommendations. A guardrail layer checks every claim against retrieved evidence, and an advisor must approve or override each result before it counts.

problem.context: Advisors work across fragmented SIS and LMS data (grades, attendance, submissions, study plans). Spotting at-risk students and choosing the next action is slow, and student data is highly sensitive.
challenges: Unify records from different source systems into one searchable form
Never expose a record the requesting user is not entitled to see
Keep AI output grounded in evidence instead of hallucinated
Avoid vendor lock-in to a single LLM provider
Keep a human accountable for every academic recommendation

approach: Separate evidence retrieval, model reasoning, validation, guardrails and human approval into distinct layers, so each can be tested and replaced on its own.

features.name: Permission-scoped access
features.description: Advisors see assigned students; faculty and department heads see their department; students see only themselves; deans get aggregate-only access; admins have no academic detail access by default.

features.name: Canonical SIS/LMS records
features.description: Source records are normalized into one academic_records table with source provenance, structured JSON facts, scope metadata and an optional embedding. A unique source_ref makes ingestion idempotent.

features.name: Scope-first hybrid retrieval
features.description: Student and department/program filters are applied in the query before any ranking. Candidates are then scored as 0.7 × embedding cosine similarity + 0.3 × keyword overlap.

features.name: Evidence-grounded output
features.description: Every profile signal and recommendation carries evidence_record_ids. Citations are built from retrieved records, not generated after the fact.

features.name: Provider-neutral model gateway
features.description: The workflow depends on an analyze()/recommend() interface. A deterministic mock is the default; any OpenAI-compatible server (Ollama, vLLM, LocalAI, OpenAI) plugs in through configuration.

features.name: Guardrails and human review
features.description: Checks unknown evidence IDs, empty retrieval or recommendations, prompt-injection-like source text and SSN-shaped identifiers. Even passing results remain advisor-reviewable.

features.name: Advisor review dashboard
features.description: React UI showing the profile, recommendations, citations, confidence and flags, with approve/override actions.

architecture.style: Layered web app with an agentic workflow and a model adapter boundary
architecture.diagram: React dashboard -> FastAPI -> Identity/authorization -> InsightWorkflow (LangGraph) -> ScopedRetriever -> SQLite or PostgreSQL+pgvector; InsightWorkflow -> ModelGateway -> Mock or OpenAI-compatible provider; results -> InsightRun + Review

layers.name: Frontend
layers.detail: React + TypeScript + Vite advisor workspace with a typed fetch client.

layers.name: API
layers.detail: FastAPI under /api/v1. Resolves the caller, authorizes the student, runs the workflow, returns validated responses.

layers.name: Authorization
layers.detail: authorize_student() runs before the workflow and again when reading a saved run. The demo identity header X-User-Email is a development seam to be replaced by OIDC/Entra claims.

layers.name: Workflow
layers.detail: LangGraph state machine over a typed InsightState: retrieve -> analyze -> recommend -> guardrail, then either awaiting_review or human_review (flagged_for_review).

layers.name: Retrieval
layers.detail: ScopedRetriever filters by student, department and program, then ranks. On PostgreSQL an HNSW cosine index narrows the permission-filtered set; on SQLite scoring runs in Python.

layers.name: Model gateway
layers.detail: MockModelGateway (deterministic, offline) or OpenAICompatibleGateway (temperature 0, JSON mode, output validated with Pydantic).

layers.name: Persistence
layers.detail: User, Student, AcademicRecord, InsightRun and Review tables. Alembic migration for PostgreSQL + pgvector.

keyBoundaries: Security boundary: scope is enforced at the API and again inside the retrieval query, so ranking can never surface out-of-scope records.
Model boundary: the workflow does not know whether reasoning is deterministic code or a remote chat model.

flows.name: Request lifecycle
steps: API resolves identity and authorizes the student
Guardrail checks grounding, flags and confidence
Dashboard shows the result for advisor review

guardrailLogic.groundedness: 1.0 only when claims exist and every claimed evidence ID was retrieved
guardrailLogic.passCondition: No flags and confidence ≥ 0.70; otherwise the run is flagged_for_review

apiSurface.purpose: Idempotently create the demo advisor, student and five synthetic records
List students filtered by the caller's role and scope
Authorize, run the graph, persist an InsightRun
Fetch a saved run after re-checking authorization
Record the advisor decision (approved or overridden)

devops: Docker Compose (API, frontend, PostgreSQL, optional Ollama profile)

keyDecisions.decision: Scope filtering before ranking
keyDecisions.reason: Relevance scoring must never be able to surface a record outside the caller's academic scope.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: Slightly more complex queries in exchange for a hard security guarantee.

keyDecisions.decision: Provider-neutral gateway with a deterministic mock default
keyDecisions.reason: Tests, golden-set evaluation and demos run with no API key, Docker or model server, and the provider can change through five env values.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: The hash-based mock embedding is a test fallback, not a semantic model.

keyDecisions.decision: SQLite and PostgreSQL+pgvector side by side
keyDecisions.reason: Zero-infrastructure local development, with a production-like vector path available.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: Two code paths for scoring; the embedding dimension must be changed together with the migration.

keyDecisions.decision: No knowledge graph in the MVP
keyDecisions.reason: Study-plan and prerequisite facts are small enough for relational rows plus JSON facts. A graph database would add operating cost before adding signal.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: Revisit Neo4j or a Postgres graph extension only when multi-hop degree-plan queries show a measurable benefit.

keyDecisions.decision: Human review is always required
keyDecisions.reason: The model drafts; guardrails check; an authorized advisor decides.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: Less automation, more accountability for a sensitive domain.

keyDecisions.decision: Treat source text as untrusted data
keyDecisions.reason: Prompt instructions tell the model record content is data, and prompt-injection-like text routes to review.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: Heuristic detection can produce false positives that cost advisor time.

engineering: Pydantic contracts validate both model output and API responses, so malformed model JSON fails loudly
Idempotent seeding and ingestion through a unique source_ref
temperature=0 and JSON mode for repeatable model output
API tests cover seed -> list -> generate -> review, plus unknown-identity rejection
Golden-set evaluation runner for regression checks
Alembic migration for the pgvector schema
Containerized with Docker Compose

workflow: View students within the advisor's authorization scope
Generate an insight for a selected student
Inspect strengths, weaknesses, engagement signals, recommendations, citations, confidence and guardrail flags
Approve or override with an optional note and 1–5 rating

records: MA202 engagement: 72% attendance, three late submissions, declining
MA202 study plan: tutoring approved, prerequisite for CS310
data.expectedOutput: At least one strength, one weakness, engagement evidence, recommendations, citations and groundedness of 1.0 with the mock provider.

outcomes: End-to-end working pipeline from authorization to retrieval, analysis, guardrails, persistence and advisor review
Runs fully offline with no key or model, and switches to a local open-weight model (for example Ollama with Qwen2.5) by configuration only
Every recommendation traces back to a cited source record
Authorization is enforced at three points: student access, retrieval query and saved-run access
limitations: X-User-Email identity header is a development seam, not production authentication
Demo data is synthetic; real connectors need schema contracts, retry/outbox, secrets management, audit logging and retention policy
Confidence is a simple heuristic, not a calibrated score
Golden set is tiny; a pilot needs 50–200 anonymized, advisor-labeled cases
nextSteps: Precomputed embeddings with retries and provider-failure monitoring
Larger labeled evaluation set with retrieval recall, recommendation validity, fairness slices, latency and cost thresholds in CI
Real SIS/LMS connectors and audit logging
Knowledge graph only if multi-hop degree-plan queries justify it

title: GraphRAG Document Intelligence Workspace
tagline: Upload documents, ask questions, get streamed answers grounded in cited passages and an explorable knowledge graph.
role: Full-stack / AI engineer (design, backend, frontend, infrastructure)
summary: A GraphRAG system that combines vector search (Qdrant) with a knowledge graph (Neo4j) so answers are grounded in source text and backed by traceable entity relationships. Documents are ingested asynchronously, retrieved with a LangGraph pipeline, and answered over Server-Sent Events with citations the user can inspect.

problem.context: Plain vector RAG retrieves isolated snippets. It misses relationships that span passages (who acquired whom, who works for which company) and gives users little way to verify where an answer came from.
challenges: Long-running document parsing, embedding and entity extraction must not block the API
Small chunks retrieve precisely but lack context; large chunks retrieve poorly
LLM answers need verifiable citations and must resist instructions hidden in documents
Re-running a failed ingestion must not duplicate vectors or graph data
Users need to see why an answer was produced, not just the text

approach: Asynchronous ingestion: the API validates and stores the upload, returns 202 Accepted, and a Celery worker does the heavy work
Hierarchical chunking: ~200-token child chunks are searched, ~1,000-token parent chunks are returned as context
Hybrid retrieval: Qdrant finds child chunks, then Neo4j relationships are traversed from entities in those chunks, bounded by a hop limit
Grounded generation: the model is told to answer only from supplied evidence, treat document text as untrusted, and cite exact IDs (P1, P2...)
Streaming UI: tokens, citations and graph data arrive as typed SSE events and render incrementally

features.name: Document ingestion
features.description: PDF, DOCX, TXT and Markdown with MIME-type, extension, size and empty-file validation, filename sanitising, UUID storage paths and SHA-256 duplicate detection.

features.name: Live ingestion progress
features.description: Per-job stage, progress, attempts and errors, polled by the UI every 1.2 s; failed jobs can be retried.

features.name: Parent/child retrieval
features.description: Child hits are grouped by parent, the best child per parent is kept, parents are ranked, and the full parent text is used as answer context.

features.name: Knowledge graph extraction
features.description: OpenAI structured output into Pydantic models; typed relationships (ACQUIRED, FOUNDED, WORKS_FOR, LOCATED_IN, PARTNERS_WITH, PRODUCES, OWNS, SUPPLIES, INVESTED_IN, RELATED_TO) with evidence, confidence and source provenance.

features.name: Bounded multi-hop graph retrieval
features.description: Defaults: 8 child results, 4 parent citations, 2 graph hops, 60 graph records, so latency and prompt size stay predictable.

features.name: Streaming grounded answers
features.description: SSE events: retrieval, graph, token, citations, done, error. Only citation IDs actually used in the answer are persisted.

features.name: Token budget management
features.description: Evidence context is built within a configured token budget before calling the model.

features.name: Interactive graph inspector
features.description: Cytoscape.js view of retrieved entities and relationships, with colour-coded entity types, fit-to-view, and edge selection showing relationship type and extraction evidence.

features.name: Citation cards
features.description: Expandable source cards showing filename, page/section, similarity score, matched passage and full parent context.

features.name: Retrieval scoping and cancellation
features.description: Users choose which ready documents to search and can abort generation mid-stream.

features.name: Persistence and audit trail
features.description: Conversations, messages and RetrievalRuns (question, vector hits, citations, graph data, latency) are stored in PostgreSQL.

features.name: Observability and health
features.description: Request IDs, structured logs (structlog), Prometheus metrics, /health/live and /health/ready (checks PostgreSQL, Redis, Qdrant, Neo4j).

features.name: Optional API-key auth
features.description: APP_AUTH_MODE=api_key enforces an X-API-Key header using constant-time comparison.

architecture.style: Layered: API -> schemas -> database -> RAG/domain services -> infrastructure adapters
architecture.diagram: Upload -> Celery job -> Parse -> Hierarchical chunks -> Qdrant vectors + Neo4j graph -> LangGraph retrieval -> Parent-context grounding -> OpenAI streaming answer -> Citations and provenance

layers.name: Frontend
layers.detail: Three-panel workspace: documents, chat, graph

layers.name: API
layers.detail: Ingest, documents, chat (SSE), graph endpoints; health and metrics

layers.name: Worker
layers.detail: Parse, chunk, embed, extract and index documents

layers.name: Relational store
layers.detail: Documents, jobs, parent/child chunks, conversations, messages, retrieval runs

layers.name: Vector store
layers.detail: Child-chunk embeddings and semantic search

layers.name: Graph store
layers.detail: Entities, relationships and provenance

layers.name: Orchestration
layers.detail: Retrieval state machine: vector + parent retrieval -> graph traversal

layers.name: Models
layers.tech: FastEmbed (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5) or OpenAI embeddings; OpenAI Responses API
layers.detail: Embeddings, entity extraction, answer generation

flows.name: Ingestion flow
steps: Embed children and upsert to Qdrant
Write graph and provenance to Neo4j

flows.name: Query flow
steps: Traverse Neo4j from mentioned entities (bounded hops)
Validate and persist citations and retrieval run

testing: Pytest unit tests (parsing, extraction, chunking, streaming contracts)

keyDecisions.decision: Parent/child chunking
keyDecisions.reason: Small chunks give precise matching; returning the larger parent gives the model enough context to answer well.

keyDecisions.decision: Deterministic IDs and idempotent ingestion
keyDecisions.reason: Retries replace Qdrant vectors and rebuild Neo4j document data instead of duplicating them.

keyDecisions.decision: Bounded graph traversal
keyDecisions.reason: Hop and record limits keep latency and prompt size predictable on densely connected graphs.

keyDecisions.decision: SSE over WebSockets
keyDecisions.reason: Streaming is one-directional, works over plain HTTP, and is simple to parse and cancel with AbortController.

keyDecisions.decision: Local embeddings by default
keyDecisions.reason: FastEmbed removes per-token embedding cost and an external dependency; OpenAI embeddings stay available as a switch.

keyDecisions.decision: Prompt-injection posture
keyDecisions.reason: Document content is explicitly treated as untrusted data and answers must cite exact evidence IDs.

keyDecisions.decision: Local React state instead of a global store
keyDecisions.reason: A single-page workflow with one stream and one graph did not justify the overhead.

engineering: Testing: Unit tests cover parsing, extraction, chunking and streaming contracts.

Deployment: Docker Compose orchestrates API, worker, PostgreSQL, Redis, Qdrant, Neo4j and frontend; the API container runs Alembic migrations before starting Uvicorn; frontend uses a three-stage standalone Next.js build.
Observability: Request IDs, structured logs, request-duration histograms, readiness checks across all four data services.

lessons.challenge: Coordinating four data stores (PostgreSQL, Redis, Qdrant, Neo4j) during ingestion
lessons.lesson: Deterministic IDs plus replace-on-retry made partial failures recoverable without cleanup scripts.

lessons.challenge: Parsing a streamed response in the browser
lessons.lesson: Wrote a custom SSE reader that buffers partial frames and dispatches typed handlers, isolated behind an API client adapter.
Citation IDs are scanned from the generated text and only valid, used ones are stored and shown.

lessons.challenge: Prompt size growth from parent chunks plus graph evidence
lessons.lesson: Added explicit token budgeting when assembling context.

limitations: Authorization is a single global API key: no users, tenants, or per-document/conversation ownership
Frontend does not send X-API-Key and has no auth flow
No runtime validation of API payloads on the frontend
Upload polling has no timeout; limited frontend test coverage
Initial migration is generated from SQLAlchemy metadata
nextSteps: Per-user/tenant ownership with JWT or OAuth, enforced on documents, conversations and retrievals
Zod validation for API and SSE payloads
Reranking and retrieval evaluation (recall, faithfulness) on a labelled question set
Component, SSE-parser and Playwright end-to-end tests

metrics.note: Only figures present in the code defaults; add measured numbers (latency, accuracy) once benchmarked.

title: MonLogement Ads Importer
tagline: A queue-driven pipeline that ingests real-estate listings from agency FTP drops (ZIP + pipe-delimited CSV), validates and geocodes them, processes their photos, and keeps a search index in sync.
summary: Real-estate agencies publish listings in a vendor feed format: a ZIP (Annonces.csv, Photos.cfg, optional images folder) and an Agences.csv uploaded over FTP. This asynchronous, fault-tolerant pipeline turns those feeds into live, searchable listings without manual work. It is the import service behind the MonLogement platform.

problem.context: Real-estate agencies publish their listings in a vendor feed format: they upload a ZIP (Annonces.csv, Photos.cfg, optional images folder) and an Agences.csv over FTP. The platform needs these listings live and searchable without manual work. Feeds are large, messy and inconsistent: mixed encodings, a custom '!#' delimiter, 300+ columns, free-text localities that don't match official names, missing or wrong coordinates, inconsistent floor data, and photos delivered in several different ways. Listings also disappear from feeds and must be removed.
challenges: Processing very large feeds without exhausting the queue or memory
Two imports for the same agency running at the same time
Removing listings that vanished from a feed without a delete flag
Unreliable coordinates and no geocoder budget
Keeping search consistent while writing many records
Dirty input: mixed encodings and a non-standard delimiter

approach: An asynchronous, fault-tolerant pipeline split into small single-purpose jobs on dedicated queues. Each stage validates its input, logs failures without blocking the rest of the feed, and hands off to the next stage.

features.name: Multi-mode photo ingestion
features.description: Supports four photo delivery modes declared in Photos.cfg: FULL (images shipped in the ZIP), DIFF (timestamped file names so only changed photos are re-uploaded), URL and AR (remote download with timeout).

features.name: Image optimisation
features.description: MIME and 40 MB size validation, scale-down to 1440px, JPEG re-encode at quality 80, and a 341x256 thumbnail generated from the already-resized image. Temporary files are always cleaned in a finally block.

features.name: Fuzzy locality matching
features.description: Normalises free-text city names (digit/letter spacing, zero-padded arrondissements, œ encoding issue), searches a Meilisearch index filtered by postal code, and falls back to SQL matching with saint/sainte to st/ste alias handling.

features.name: Geocoding and coordinate sanity checks
features.description: Supplied coordinates are verified against the official commune boundary (geo.api.gouv.fr, with special handling for Paris/Lyon/Marseille arrondissements). Bad or missing ones are replaced by a random point inside the commune polygon (ray-casting; largest polygon for MultiPolygons) with a small jitter, and flagged as auto-filled.

features.name: Domain mapping
features.description: Maps agency vocabulary to internal types (e.g. 'maison-villa' to house, 'vente de prestige' to sell), converts kWh and GES values to A-G energy and gas classes, derives facilities (lift, pool, cellar, parking count...), and resolves French administrative levels from postal codes including Corsica 2A/2B and overseas departments.

features.name: Data-quality rules
features.description: Rows are skipped with a precise log line when postal code, locality, reference, price or agency is invalid; inconsistent floor / total-floor pairs are nulled; construction year is range-checked; HTML descriptions are sanitised on write with Purifier.

features.name: Error observability
features.description: Row and image failures are persisted to an AdsImportingErrorLog table (type, message, stack trace, file, line, batch id, agency and technical id context) and pruned by a daily command.

features.name: Agency hierarchy support
features.description: Listings are attributed to the child agency named in the row, falling back to the parent feed owner, and the user account falls back along the same chain. Cleanup covers both the agency and its sub-agencies.

architecture.style: Event-driven job pipeline with scheduled polling

layers.name: Scan
layers.detail: Walks the FTP incoming directory, maps each folder to an agency via its ftp_username, and chains an agencies import and a ZIP processing job. Capped at 10 files per run and unique-locked to avoid overlapping runs.

layers.name: Agencies sync
layers.detail: Cleans the Agences.csv, streams it with Spatie Simple Excel and fans it out as a batch of 1000-row chunk jobs.

layers.name: Unpack & validate
layers.detail: Archives the ZIP under a dated processed folder, extracts it to a timestamped directory, validates required files, reads the photo mode from Photos.cfg, and normalises the CSV (encoding detection, unsupported chars, custom delimiter).

layers.name: Self-scheduling batches
layers.detail: Creates batches of 5 chunk jobs x 500 rows, then re-dispatches itself 30s later until the file is exhausted, so the queue is never flooded. The last iteration schedules cleanup.

layers.name: Row processing
layers.detail: Per row: validates, maps types, resolves region/department from postal code, matches the locality, resolves coordinates, then upserts the listing and its facilities inside a DB transaction and indexes it.

layers.name: Image processing
layers.detail: Resizes, recompresses and thumbnails up to 10 photos per listing and uploads them to object storage.

layers.name: Reconciliation cleanup
layers.detail: Deletes listings no longer present in the feed (with their images and index entries) and resets the import flag for the next run.

scheduledMaintenance: Cleanup of extracted directories older than a week (daily)

challenges.challenge: Processing very large feeds without exhausting the queue or memory
challenges.solution: Streamed CSV reading with fgetcsv, 500-row chunk jobs grouped into small batches, and a self-rescheduling batch dispatcher with a 30s delay instead of enqueueing everything at once.
challenges.outcome: Predictable memory use and back-pressure regardless of file size; failures are isolated to a chunk (allowFailures).

challenges.challenge: Two imports for the same agency running at the same time
challenges.solution: ShouldBeUnique on ScanJob and on the ZIP job (keyed by agency UUID, 1h lock), WithoutOverlapping middleware keyed by agency on chunk jobs, and chained jobs to preserve agencies-before-listings order.
challenges.outcome: No duplicate or interleaved writes per agency.

challenges.challenge: Removing listings that vanished from a feed without a delete flag
challenges.solution: Mark-and-sweep: every upsert sets is_imported = true; the final cleanup job deletes records still false for that agency tree (chunks of 1000, images deleted from storage in batches of 100 via dedicated jobs, DB rows and search index removed in a transaction), then resets the flag.
challenges.outcome: Catalogue always mirrors the latest feed, and storage does not accumulate orphaned photos.

challenges.challenge: Unreliable coordinates and no geocoder budget
challenges.solution: Validate against official boundaries, otherwise generate a point inside the polygon so map pins never land outside the right town.
challenges.outcome: All listings are map-ready and consistently placed; approximate points are marked with coordinates_auto_fill.

challenges.challenge: Keeping search consistent while writing many records
challenges.solution: Wrap writes in withoutSyncingToSearch, then trigger a single searchable() call after the listing and its facilities are saved.
challenges.outcome: One index update per listing instead of several.

challenges.challenge: Dirty input: mixed encodings and a non-standard delimiter
challenges.solution: Line-by-line encoding detection (UTF-8 / ISO-8859-1 / Windows-1252), conversion to UTF-8, stripping of invalid bytes, and delimiter rewriting to a single character before parsing.
challenges.outcome: Accents and special characters survive end to end.

engineering: Single-responsibility jobs with explicit constructors and typed parameters
Dedicated queues per workload type so heavy image work cannot starve CSV processing
Idempotent upserts keyed on the agency technical id
DB transactions around listing writes
External HTTP calls with timeouts and retries
Scheduled housekeeping commands for disk and log growth
Configuration-driven city code mapping (composite cities enum + config)

metrics.note: Fill with real production numbers before publishing; none are derivable from the code.

title: MonLogement — French Administrative Boundaries to Mapbox Vector Tiles
tagline: A Laravel job pipeline that turns the official French administrative dataset into regions, departments and communes in the database, and publishes their borders as Mapbox vector tiles.
summary: MonLogement lets users search listings by region, department and commune and see those areas as borders on a map. I built the pipeline that extracts the official French boundary dataset, converts and cleans it with GDAL, stores each area with its bounding box, and pushes the shapes to Mapbox as a tileset so borders render as fast vector tiles instead of heavy GeoJSON.

problem.context: Area search and area borders need authoritative geometry for roughly 35,000 communes plus departments and regions. The official source is a large national GeoPackage in the Lambert-93 projection, while Mapbox expects WGS84 lon/lat. Serving the raw polygons to the browser as GeoJSON would be far too heavy, and the work is too long-running to do inside a web request.
challenges: Official data ships as one large GeoPackage with many layers in EPSG:2154 (Lambert-93), not the EPSG:4326 that web maps use
Commune polygons are too large to send to the browser as plain GeoJSON
The app needs each area's name, code, level and bounding box for search and for fitting the map view
Mapbox tileset sources expect line-delimited GeoJSON, not a single FeatureCollection
Conversion, upload and tile publishing are long-running and must be retryable without blocking the app
Credentials for the Mapbox API must stay out of code and logs

approach: Treat the dataset as an ETL pipeline of small queued Laravel jobs, each wrapping one GDAL or HTTP step, so every stage can fail, retry and be re-run on its own.
Reproject once at extraction (EPSG:2154 to EPSG:4326, XY only, 6-decimal coordinate precision) and keep everything downstream in WGS84.
Split the output by purpose: attributes and bounding boxes go to the database for search; shapes go to Mapbox as vector tiles for rendering.

features.name: Layer extraction from the official GeoPackage
features.description: ogr2ogr loops over the layers of the IGN Admin Express GeoPackage (region, departement, commune, epci, arrondissement, canton and their chef-lieu point layers) and writes one GeoJSON per layer, reprojected to EPSG:4326 with a fixed coordinate precision to shrink file size.

features.name: Layer inspection before processing
features.description: ogrinfo summary mode is used to check feature counts, fields and geometry types of each file before the import jobs rely on them.

features.name: Bounding boxes in the database
features.description: An ogr2ogr SQLite-dialect query exports name, code, level and ST_MinX / ST_MinY / ST_MaxX / ST_MaxY per area to CSV, which the importer loads so the map can fit to an area and search can filter spatially without reading geometries.

features.name: Line-delimited GeoJSON for tiling
features.description: Each level (regions, departments, communes) is converted to GeoJSONSeq, one feature per line, which is the format a Mapbox Tiling Service tileset source accepts.

features.name: Tileset source upload
features.description: The line-delimited file is uploaded as a multipart request to the Mapbox Tilesets API (sources endpoint) from a Laravel job, one source per level.

features.name: Vector tile borders on the map
features.description: Published tilesets are drawn as line and fill layers in Mapbox GL, so region, department and commune borders stream as tiles at the zoom levels the user is viewing.

architecture.style: Sequential queued job pipeline wrapping GDAL command-line tools and the Mapbox Tilesets API
architecture.diagram: Admin Express GeoPackage (EPSG:2154) -> ogr2ogr per layer -> GeoJSON (EPSG:4326) -> [bbox CSV -> database] and [GeoJSONSeq -> Mapbox tileset source -> tileset -> vector tiles -> Mapbox GL layers]

layers.name: Source data
layers.detail: Official edition dated 2025-09-16, containing administrative layers and their chef-lieu points.

layers.name: Extraction job
layers.detail: Iterates the layer list and writes one reprojected GeoJSON per layer.

layers.name: Inspection and bbox job
layers.detail: Verifies each file and exports name, code, level and bounding box to CSV.

layers.name: Import job
layers.detail: Loads areas and bounding boxes into the area tables used by search and map fitting.

layers.name: Conversion job
layers.detail: Produces line-delimited GeoJSON for each level.

layers.name: Publish job
layers.detail: Uploads each level as a tileset source over HTTP so Mapbox can build vector tiles from it.

layers.name: Map rendering
layers.detail: Vector tile source with line layers for borders and highlight on the selected area.

keyBoundaries: Database holds attributes and bounding boxes for search; Mapbox holds geometry for rendering. The app never loads polygons just to draw a border.
GDAL steps run as external processes behind jobs, so a conversion failure is a failed job with a log, not a failed web request.

flows.name: Boundary refresh pipeline
steps: Download the new Admin Express GeoPackage
Extract each layer to GeoJSON in EPSG:4326
Export name, code, level and bounding box to CSV
Import areas and bounding boxes into the database
Convert each level to line-delimited GeoJSON
Upload each file as a Mapbox tileset source
Publish the tileset and use it as a vector source in Mapbox GL

source: IGN Admin Express (official French administrative boundaries)

keyDecisions.decision: Vector tiles instead of serving GeoJSON to the browser
keyDecisions.reason: Commune borders for the whole country are far too large as GeoJSON. Tiles load only what the current view needs and simplify automatically by zoom level.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: Depends on an external tiling service and a publish step whenever the boundaries change.

keyDecisions.decision: Reproject once with ogr2ogr at extraction
keyDecisions.reason: Every later stage works in EPSG:4326, so the database, the CSV and the tiles all agree and no runtime reprojection is needed.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: Source geometry in Lambert-93 is not kept in the app; re-extract from the GeoPackage if it is ever needed.

keyDecisions.decision: Fixed coordinate precision (6 decimals)
keyDecisions.reason: About 0.1 m of precision is more than a border needs and keeps files and tiles much smaller.

keyDecisions.decision: Store bounding boxes in the database
keyDecisions.reason: Fit-to-area and spatial filtering use four numbers per area instead of loading a polygon.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: Boxes must be regenerated with each dataset refresh.

keyDecisions.decision: Small queued jobs per step
keyDecisions.reason: Each GDAL or HTTP call can be retried or re-run on its own, and the long work stays off the web request path.
keyDecisions.tradeoff: More job classes and a need to keep stage order explicit.

challenges.challenge: National dataset in a projected coordinate system
challenges.solution: Reproject to EPSG:4326 and drop Z/M dimensions at extraction, with a fixed coordinate precision.
challenges.outcome: Files load directly into Mapbox and the database without further conversion.

challenges.challenge: Tileset source rejects a single large FeatureCollection

title: Blindlove — AI Matchmaking Engine
tagline: A hybrid matching system for an anonymous dating app: weighted preference filtering narrows the pool, then Redis vector search ranks candidates by semantic profile similarity.
role: Lead Backend Developer and AI Architect
summary: Blindlove is an anonymous dating platform. I designed and built its matchmaking backend: user bios, interests and preferences are turned into vector embeddings with Hugging Face sentence-transformers and indexed in Redis Stack. A hybrid algorithm combines weighted-preference filtering, bitmap interest scoring, cosine similarity and K-nearest-neighbour vector search, and the best matches are cached in Redis for fast retrieval.

problem.context: In an anonymous dating app there are no photos or visible profiles to browse, so match quality depends almost entirely on how well the system understands what a person wrote and prefers. Filters alone match on declared fields and miss semantic similarity between free-text bios and interests, and the matching has to stay fast for many concurrent users.
challenges: Go beyond exact-field filtering and match on the meaning of bios and interests
Keep matching fast and scalable for many concurrent users
Keep embeddings fresh when a user changes their profile
Run real-time chat and notifications across multiple Node.js processes without duplicate connections or duplicate jobs
Support multiple languages across every application layer

approach: Pool first: narrow candidates with general filtration using weighted preferences
Score with bitmap interests and cosine similarity
Re-rank semantically with Redis Vector Search over Hugging Face embeddings
Store top matches per user in Redis sorted lists with their similarity scores
Process match requests through a Redis queue so matching never blocks the API

title: Roomco — Legacy Platform Modernization
tagline: Migrating a legacy Express.js and Node 12 platform to a NestJS modular monolith, merging two Express apps into one, extracting moderation microservices, and modernizing the MongoDB data layer.
status: Backend migration delivered; Firebase-to-MongoDB user consolidation planned as a roadmap
summary: Roomco is a social and chat application for young users. Its backend had grown on Node 12 with outdated dependencies, two separate Express apps (one for the chat sockets, one for the API), a legacy MongoDB version and weak data structures. I led the move to a NestJS and TypeScript modular monolith on a current Node.js version, merged the two apps into one, extracted content moderation into independent microservices, upgraded and cleaned up MongoDB, and designed the roadmap for consolidating users from Firebase and the legacy Mongo database into a better-structured, performance-optimized schema.

problem.context: The platform ran on an aging stack: Node 12 with outdated dependencies, plain Express.js without static typing, and separate Express applications for the socket server and the REST API. Users lived in two places, a Firebase database and a legacy MongoDB with outdated and poorly designed data structures. Each of these made the system harder to change safely and added operational complexity.
challenges: Upgrade Node.js from 12 to 22 and resolve outdated or incompatible dependencies without breaking behaviour
Migrate from Express.js to NestJS and TypeScript while the product kept running
Remove the complexity of running a separate chat-socket Express app alongside the API Express app
Isolate heavy content moderation (media and text) from the main application
Upgrade a legacy MongoDB version and fix outdated, badly structured data
Plan the merge of users from Firebase and legacy MongoDB into one optimized structure
Bring the development team along with the new architecture

approach: Migrate incrementally to NestJS with TypeScript under a documented migration strategy supervised across the team
Merge the chat socket app and the API app into a single NestJS modular monolith instead of splitting into more services
Extract only what benefits from independent scaling, content moderation, into separate microservices
Upgrade MongoDB and repair data structures, then roadmap the user consolidation from Firebase and legacy Mongo
Document the patterns and train the team so the new architecture is maintainable
